title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Girl in a Mill: Maggie\'s Hunger

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the next hour we're going to spend time with one of the most extraordinary novels in the English language.
George Eliot published The Mill on the Floss in 1860, and it has never quite let its readers go.
It's a novel about childhood, about a girl's ferocious hunger for a life bigger than the one on offer, and about the price the world charges for that hunger.
Today we begin where the novel begins — with Maggie Tulliver, the mill, the river, and a family's slow unravelling.
Joining me today are three readers who know this novel intimately and have very different things to say about it.
Oliver Trevelyan has given his voice to more classic novels on audio than perhaps anyone alive.
He hears prose the way a musician hears a score — for its rhythm, its comic timing, its silences.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most formidable close readers of Victorian fiction working today.
Edmund reads novels as moral investigations — stories of character tested by the world — and he brings that clarity to bear on everything Eliot does.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She brings the reader's eye — the experience of the page, the sentences that stop you cold, the characters you feel you've actually known.
So — Maggie Tulliver, and the question the novel asks from its first pages: what does a girl do with a mind like that?
The first thing you notice, when you actually read the opening of this novel aloud, is the dreaming quality of it.
Eliot opens with a narrator watching the river — watching the mill wheel turning — and it feels like memory before it feels like story.
And then Maggie arrives, this small dark child sitting on a sack of meal with her feet dangling, and she is so completely, arrestingly alive on the page.
Eliot has this gift — and it's almost unfair — of making you feel you've always known a character, within about three sentences.
With Maggie, that feeling arrives almost immediately.
And Eliot gives us Mrs Tulliver fretting about Maggie's hair — this dark, tangled, ungovernable hair — as a kind of symbol right from the start.
It stands for everything about Maggie that refuses to be tidied into what the world expects of a girl.
What strikes me every time I return to those early chapters is the sheer comedy of the Tulliver household.
Mr Tulliver is one of the great comic figures in Victorian fiction — this bluff, passionate, thoroughly unreasonable man who is certain he's in the right about everything.
And yet Eliot makes you love him.
His pride in Maggie's quickness — and his simultaneous bewilderment that such a quick child could be a girl — is both funny and a little heartbreaking.
He says something to that effect quite early — that she's too cute for a woman, that it's a pity she wasn't born a lad.
"It's a pity but what she'd been the lad — she'd ha' been a match for the lawyers, she would."
And there it is — the entire novel's tragedy compressed into a father's offhand compliment.
He can see what she is, and yet the best he can imagine for her is what she might have been, if she'd been born a boy.
I think one has to be precise about the nature of Maggie's hunger, because Eliot is.
It is not primarily a social grievance — it is a spiritual and intellectual hunger.
Maggie wants to be loved, yes — passionately, extravagantly loved.
But she also wants to understand.
She wants the books in her father's study, she wants Philip Wakem to talk to her about music and painting, she wants a larger life than St Ogg's can offer.
Eliot is quite careful to show us that the deprivation is not merely material — it is a deprivation of the spirit.
Thomas à Kempis, when Maggie discovers him in the third book, is not simply a coping mechanism.
It is a genuine philosophical response to the question of what a person does when the world refuses to give them what they need.
Whether Eliot endorses that response is, of course, another matter entirely.
Edmund is right about the à Kempis moment — it's one of the most quietly devastating things in the novel.
But I want to go back to the child Maggie for a moment, because there's something Eliot does in those early chapters that I find quite astonishing from a craft perspective.
She gives Maggie this almost violent emotional life — the rages, the sudden tenderness, the running away to the gypsies — and she renders it with absolute sympathy.
But she also renders it with the lightest possible touch of comedy.
The gypsy episode — where Maggie imagines she'll become their queen and is instead comprehensively disillusioned — is one of the funniest passages of childhood in Victorian fiction.
And yet Eliot never laughs at Maggie.
She laughs with her, and that distinction is everything.
That's exactly it — Eliot extends to Maggie the same quality of attention she asks us to extend.
I think that's why the novel feels so personal to so many readers.
There's a moment early in the novel where Eliot steps back and says, almost directly to the reader, that she is giving us the history of unfashionable families.
"In these Latin-named villages, the farmers and millers and weavers seemed to suffer and to be moved by no other passion than the love of gain."
And then she says — and this is the move that opens the whole book up — that the suffering of such people is no less real for being unrecorded.
That's the ethical claim at the heart of the novel.
Maggie's life matters.
Her hunger matters.
Miss Woodcourt has identified the crux of it, I think.
And it connects to something Dr Johnson understood very well — that literature's highest function is to enlarge our sympathies.
What Eliot does in the childhood books is not merely charming.
She is building the moral architecture for everything that follows.
Every eccentricity of Maggie's character that will later cause her harm is also, Eliot shows us, evidence of her remarkable nature.
The passionate attachments, the impulsiveness, the need for more than St Ogg's can give — these are not flaws to be corrected.
They are the signs of a soul.
A soul the world will spend three volumes trying to diminish.
We'll be looking at exactly how that pressure builds — and what Maggie does with it — as we move through the novel today.
Coming up next: the Tulliver family and what Eliot sees in the comedy of provincial life — and what it costs.

segments.title: The Pleasure and the Pain: Eliot's Comic Mastery

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're spending an hour with one of the great novels of the Victorian age — George Eliot's deeply personal, deeply funny, and ultimately devastating masterpiece.
We have three remarkable readers with us, each of whom brings something irreplaceable to this conversation.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears the prose as performance, and he's going to make sure we hear it that way too.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose readings of Victorian fiction are always as morally serious as they are elegant.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first encountered this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered — which I mean as the highest possible compliment.
We're opening with something that doesn't always get the attention it deserves: George Eliot's comedy.
The Mill on the Floss is often remembered for its tragedy, but it is also one of the funniest novels in the language — and the comedy and the pain are inseparable.
The first thing you notice when you sit down to read this novel aloud — really aloud, performing it — is that Eliot has an absolutely lethal comic ear.
The Dodson sisters alone would sustain a lesser writer's entire career.
Mrs. Glegg, Mrs. Pullet, Mrs. Deane — they are a complete taxonomy of provincial respectability and wounded vanity.
And Eliot loves them.
That's what makes the comedy so rich — there's no contempt in it.
Think of the scene where Mrs. Pullet weeps over her new bonnet — the bonnet she hasn't worn yet, the bonnet that is being saved, essentially, for a grander occasion than life will likely provide.
That is a perfectly engineered comic set-piece, but it also tells you everything about a certain kind of life — a life organised around appearances and the fear of losing status.
Oliver is absolutely right about the generosity, and I think that is the key word.
Eliot never writes about the Dodsons from above.
She writes from inside their world — inside their logic — which is why the comedy never curdles into satire.
The Dodsons have a code, a genuine moral code, however narrow it may be — and Eliot respects that narrowness as a form of seriousness.
She tells us, in her own voice, that the Dodsons' way of life had a dignity and a consistency that we might do well not to dismiss.
I find that authorial candour rather bracing in an age when provincial life is so easily mocked.
What strikes me — and it struck me the first time I read this, aged about fifteen — is that the comedy is never entirely comfortable.
You're laughing, and then suddenly you feel the laugh catch in your throat.
Think about Mr. Tulliver.
He is, on one level, a comic figure — the blustering, litigious miller who can't stop fighting battles he will certainly lose.
There's genuine comic pleasure in watching him declare war on Wakem, a man better equipped in every conceivable way for the fight.
But the comedy doesn't protect you from the devastation that follows.
By the time Tulliver has his stroke and lies helpless and humiliated, you realise the comedy was always a kind of tragic overture.
That's beautifully put — the comic as tragic overture.
And I think it's the narrator's voice that performs this doubling most brilliantly.
Eliot's narrator can be wickedly funny in a single subordinate clause, and then turn around in the main clause and break your heart.
There's a passage early in the novel where she describes Mr. Tulliver's conviction that the world was not run on sound commercial principles — and the cadence of it is pure comedy.
"It was Mr. Tulliver's weakness to be more litigious than was consistent with a sound judicial mind."
That rhythm — the mock-solemn pause before the devastating qualification — is the Eliot comic signature.
You can hear Johnson in it, a little — the balanced sentence that conceals a stiletto.
The Johnsonian comparison is well-placed — Eliot was a very careful reader of Johnson.
But I want to say something about Bob Jakin, because he tends to be undervalued in discussions of the comedy.
Bob is a genuinely original comic creation — the roving packman, cheerfully dishonest in small things, utterly loyal in great ones.
He is, in some ways, the healthiest moral intelligence in the novel — and he is also very funny.
The scene where he brings Maggie a parcel of books — having selected them himself, having thought about her — is one of the most touching comic scenes in Victorian fiction.
Goodness wearing the costume of roguery.
Bob Jakin is one of those characters I would follow into a different novel entirely.
But what I keep coming back to in this segment is the question of what it costs Maggie to live inside this comedy.
Because the world that is so richly comic to us — the Dodsons, the lawsuits, the social rituals — is the world that is crushing her.
There's a moment where Eliot writes — and I'm quoting from memory, so forgive any small imprecision — that Maggie's nature was too large for the world that claimed her.
That line does something the comedy alone can't do: it makes the reader complicit in the tragedy.
We have been enjoying St. Ogg's as a comic spectacle, and then Eliot reminds us that someone is actually trapped inside it.
That's the move that separates Eliot from all the Trollopes and Gaskells who are very good at the comedy of provincial life.
She can deploy the Dickensian grotesque — and she does, with the Dodsons — but she won't let you stay there.
The comedy is always in the service of something larger and darker.
When I perform the Dodson chapters — and I have, more than once — I try to find the exact register where the audience is laughing and anxious at the same time.
Because that double register is where Eliot lives as a writer.
The double register — that's a phrase we'll keep returning to today, I suspect.
Comedy as the grammar of tragedy, or perhaps tragedy as the secret logic of everything that made us laugh.
In our next segment, we're going to move deeper into the novel's heart — into the childhood of Maggie and Tom, and what Eliot does with memory and loss.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Character Tested: The Moral Imagination of The Mill

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into one of the great moral dramas of Victorian fiction.
George Eliot sets her characters impossible tests — of loyalty, of self-denial, of desire — and watches them fail or endure with extraordinary compassion.
With me today are three readers who bring very different eyes to this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more classic novels aloud than perhaps anyone alive, and he hears the rhythms of Eliot's prose the way a musician hears a score.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a critic for whom character and moral imagination are the heart of any great novel.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a reader who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
Our theme today: Character Tested — what does The Mill on the Floss reveal about how people break, bend, and sometimes hold under pressure?
The first thing I'd say about this novel — and I say it as someone who has read it aloud many times — is that Eliot never lets her characters off the hook.
Not even the ones we adore.
Maggie Tulliver is the most vivid, most brilliant character in the novel, possibly one of the most vivid in all of Victorian fiction.
And yet Eliot insists on showing us her weaknesses as clearly as her gifts.
There's a moment in the novel where Eliot reflects on how Maggie's great need for love makes her vulnerable — how she reaches for approval and affection with a kind of desperate hunger.
Eliot writes that Maggie had "that girl's nature which longs for superior strength — to lean upon and be guided."
That phrase catches something absolutely essential about Maggie — and about why she fails when Stephen Guest enters the picture.
She is not stupid. She is not wicked. She is catastrophically susceptible to being admired by someone she admires.
Oliver is quite right, though I would frame it rather differently.
The Mill on the Floss is, at its centre, a novel about the relationship between character and circumstance — and what Eliot insists upon, rather unfashionably, is that character is fate.
She takes the phrase almost directly from Novalis — but she means something very specific by it.
Maggie's doom is not imposed from outside. It flows from who she is — from her passionate nature, her hunger for the ideal, her inability to endure ordinary life.
Eliot sets this out quite explicitly in the later chapters, when she reflects on the nature of moral struggle.

She says of Maggie that she was "not a creature of conventional morality" but that she yearned for "something beyond the daily round" — that the conflict between duty and longing was not merely personal but almost cosmic in its weight.
That is the moral imagination of the novel in miniature.
Eliot does not offer easy consolation. She asks whether a noble nature, badly formed by an ungenerous world, can survive — and her answer is extraordinarily honest.
What strikes me most — every time I read it — is how early the moral testing begins.
We think of the great crisis as the elopement with Stephen Guest, or the flood.
But Eliot begins testing Maggie in childhood — with the hair-cutting scene, with the gypsies, with her treatment of Tom.
These early scenes are written with such comedy and warmth that we almost miss what Eliot is doing.
She is showing us a child whose moral instincts are genuine but whose self-control is desperately, painfully undeveloped.

There's a line I can never shake — when Eliot reflects on Maggie's childhood reading and says she had been "nourishing herself on a few ill-chosen books" and that her mind was "full of contradictory elements."
That image of the ill-nourished mind — brilliant but badly fed — explains everything that follows.
The moral crises of adulthood are seeded in the deprivations of childhood. Eliot is absolutely clear about that.
Caroline's point about the childhood scenes is something I find fascinating from a purely performative standpoint.
When I read those early chapters aloud, there's a tonal quality that is genuinely comic — high comic, almost Dickensian in its relish.
The Dodson aunts — Mrs. Glegg, Mrs. Pullet — they are masterpieces of provincial comedy, and Eliot clearly adores them even as she skewers them.
But then the key is that this comic world is also a morally claustrophobic one — and it is the world that forms Maggie.
Tom inherits it completely — he becomes everything the Dodsons value: propriety, hard dealing, the sanctity of the debt paid.
Maggie rebels against it and is destroyed — partly by the world, but partly, as Edmund says, by who she is.
The scene where Tom casts Maggie out after the affair with Stephen Guest — that is the Dodson world's verdict delivered by her own brother.
And it is utterly devastating precisely because Tom is not entirely wrong.
Oliver has put his finger on something I consider central to Eliot's moral achievement in this novel.
Tom Tulliver is not a villain. He is, in many respects, a model of a certain kind of English virtue.
He honours his father's debt when the law does not require it. He rebuilds the family's name through industry and self-discipline.
And yet his treatment of Maggie is merciless in a way that Eliot renders with complete moral clarity.
She writes of Tom that he had "a mind not to be enriched by reflection" — a terrible epitaph for a man of genuine goodness.
There is the tragedy in miniature: virtues that will not flex, a loyalty that hardens into cruelty, and the narrowness that passes for moral order in St Ogg's.
Eliot is not sentimental about any of it. She asks us to hold both truths at once — Tom's real worth, and his real failure of imagination.
The question of imagination — moral imagination — is exactly where I want to dwell for a moment.
Because I think Eliot is doing something very bold in this novel — she is arguing that the capacity for sympathy, for entering another person's experience, is a moral faculty.
And it can be stunted by a bad education, a narrow world, a life without books or music or genuine conversation.
Philip Wakem understands Maggie in a way Tom never can — and it's precisely because Philip has been forced, by illness and isolation, to live in his inner life.

There's that deeply tender passage in the Red Deeps where Philip says to Maggie that she will always be struggling — that she is "a poor hungry shivering, homeless dog" who cannot be satisfied with a bone.
He sees her more clearly than she sees herself, and there is an ache in that scene that stays with you.
Eliot rewards imaginative sympathy in her characters — and she punishes its absence with something very close to tragedy.
The Red Deeps scenes are some of the most beautifully written in the novel — and some of the most affecting to read aloud.
There's a quality of secrecy, of stolen happiness, that Eliot renders with extraordinary delicacy.
And yet — and this is where I think Eliot is genuinely courageous — she doesn't let us rest in the romance of it.
Philip's love for Maggie is real, but it is also possessive. His grief at losing her to Stephen Guest is genuine — and tinged with resentment.
Nobody in this novel is simply good or simply bad. That is Eliot's great gift — and it's what makes the final catastrophe so overwhelming.
When Maggie and Tom are finally reconciled — in the flood, in the boat, in those last moments — it's because all the complexity falls away.
Eliot writes that "the boat reappeared — but brother and sister had gone down in an embrace never to be parted."
I defy anyone to read that aloud without something shifting in the throat.
The ending is one of the most debated in Victorian fiction — and I confess I have changed my view of it over the years.
I once thought Eliot had cheated — that the flood was a deus ex machina, a way of escaping the novel's own moral logic.
I no longer think that.
The flood is the external world intruding on characters who have been living too entirely in their inner worlds — and it strips everything back to the primal bond.
The reconciliation of Tom and Maggie is not sentimental. It is Eliot recognising that beneath all the moral complexity — the failures, the pride, the severity — there is love.
And the tragedy is that the world of St Ogg's, with all its propriety and its ledgers, can only make room for that love at the moment of death.
That is a genuinely tragic structure. Not melodrama — tragedy, in the proper sense.
I want to come back to one thing Edmund said earlier — about duty and longing — because I think it's the emotional spine of the whole novel.
Maggie's great moral crisis — the drift downriver with Stephen Guest — is so brilliantly constructed because Eliot insists that Maggie is not passive.
She chooses, at every moment, and then she fails to choose, and then she chooses again.
The horror of the Stephen Guest episode is that Maggie's will is overwhelmed not by violence or deceit, but by music and attention and the ordinary human need to be loved.
And when she does return — when she chooses duty over happiness — the world punishes her for the weakness and refuses to credit the choice.
That's what I find so quietly devastating about this novel — the inadequacy of the world's moral vocabulary for what Maggie actually is.
St Ogg's has no word for a woman who sins, suffers, repents, and endures — except, bluntly, ruined.
That word — ruined — and all its terrible weight in the world of St Ogg's.
I think what our conversation today has uncovered is the depth of Eliot's moral seriousness — and her refusal to make that seriousness comfortable.
She tests her characters — Tom, Maggie, Philip — until we understand not just what they do but why, and what the world made them.
Thank you, Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — a rich conversation that we will continue in the next segment.

segments.title: A Debt Unpayable: Mr Tulliver\'s Ruin and Grace

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've spent time with the Dodson sisters and their magnificent codes of propriety, and with Maggie's hungry, restless childhood.
Now we turn to the catastrophe at the heart of the novel's first half — Mr Tulliver's ruin.
The lawsuit, the bankruptcy, the humiliation — and then something unexpected: a strange, fierce, almost Biblical dignity in the way Tulliver bears his loss.
Oliver, you've voiced Tulliver in the audiobook — what does this section feel like from the inside?
Tulliver is one of the great tragic-comic creations in English fiction, and I mean that as the highest compliment.
He's a man who carries enormous dignity — genuine dignity — inside a personality that keeps making catastrophic errors.
And the ruin sequence — the bankruptcy, the auction, the creditors walking through the mill — Eliot writes it with this almost unbearable compression.
What undoes me every time is the moment Tulliver asks Tom to write in the family Bible.
He wants his hatred of Wakem written down — registered — as if the page of scripture makes it a covenant with God.
It's grotesque, it's magnificent, and it's absolutely Tulliver.
That Bible scene stops me every single time.
Because Eliot gives you the exact words Tom writes — and they have this raw, ungrammatical fury.
Something to the effect of: this is written down so that my son may know that his father was a man who paid his debts, and that Wakem was his ruin.
And Tulliver wants it known — wants it witnessed — that his enemy's name stands condemned in Holy Writ.
It's a debt of honour dressed up as a curse, and it's heartbreaking precisely because you understand exactly why he does it.
He has almost nothing left — and this terrible, wrongheaded gesture is what he has instead of justice.
The Bible inscription is what separates Eliot from her contemporaries.
A lesser writer would have made Tulliver's ruin merely pathetic — a cautionary tale about imprudence.
Eliot insists that Tulliver is culpable — his litigiousness, his vanity about Tom's education — these are real failings of character.
And yet she will not strip him of his dignity.
That is the moral imagination at work — not the political one, the moral one.
The scene where he pays off the family creditors — using Mrs Tulliver's precious stored capital — and then sinks back exhausted into his chair, having done what he set out to do.
He has honoured the debt, and the honour costs him everything that remains.
Edmund's right, and I want to add something about the performative dimension of all this.
Tulliver is a man who needs witnesses.
The mill, the land, the lawsuit — these are all public things, things seen and known in the community of St Ogg's.
When he falls, he falls in full view — and when he recovers any portion of his honour, that too must be public.
The moment that absolutely destroys me as a performer — and I've read it a dozen times — is when Tulliver meets Wakem on horseback and the old violence comes back.
He thrashes Wakem with his riding whip — a man he depends upon for his livelihood — and it is simultaneously the most destructive and the most honest thing he has ever done.
And then the stroke that kills him arrives almost immediately — as if his body knew the account was finally settled.
That sequence — the attack on Wakem, the fall, the deathbed — is written with such velocity.
Eliot doesn't linger; she moves with Tulliver's own momentum, and it feels like fate executing itself.
What stays with me is his dying words to Tom — the return to the mill in his mind.
He speaks of the old days, of his father's mill, of belonging to this place.
And Eliot writes something like: 'You'll have the mill again — and I've given you the chance.'
He gives Tom the mill as his final gift — all that striving and pain resolved into that one bequest.
It's a father's whole life handed to his son in a sentence.
That deathbed is, I think, one of the great deathbed scenes in Victorian fiction — and the competition is stiff.
What Eliot refuses to do — and this is where her moral rigour shows — is to redeem Tulliver's faults at death.
He dies still wrong about Wakem, still convinced of his own righteousness.
But Eliot asks us — and this is the extraordinary demand she makes of the reader — to love him precisely as he is.
Not the improved, corrected, moralised version of Tulliver — the real one, errors and all.
Dr Johnson said that the purpose of fiction is to teach the reader by delightful means — but Eliot asks something harder.
She asks the reader to extend sympathy without requiring the object of that sympathy to deserve it in any tidy, satisfying way.
Edmund has hit it exactly — and I think the actor's version of that insight is this: Tulliver is fully consistent.
He is the same man in prosperity and ruin, in violence and tenderness.
And the extraordinary thing about Eliot — the thing I notice when reading him aloud — is that his speech rhythms never change.
He speaks in the same blunt, slightly knotted cadences whether he's arranging Tom's schooling or lying on his deathbed.
That is a novelist who completely inhabits her character — who doesn't reach for elevation at the emotional climaxes.
Tulliver as a man of absolute consistency — flawed to the end, and loved for it.
There's something almost tragic in the way his very nature — that stubborn, proud, litigious nature — is also what holds the novel's moral world together.
We'll return after the break to look at Tom Tulliver — the son who inherits the debt, and what repaying it costs him.

segments.title: The Rift Between Them: Sibling Love and Duty

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been circling the great emotional core of this novel — and now we arrive at it directly.
The relationship between Maggie and Tom Tulliver: a bond of extraordinary tenderness, and extraordinary cruelty.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — you've all spent time with this novel, and I know you each feel this relationship differently.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because I suspect you have strong instincts about Tom as a dramatic creation.
Strong instincts is one way of putting it.
Tom Tulliver is one of the great dramatic challenges in the English novel — because he is so thoroughly, so consistently, so magnificently in the wrong.
And yet you cannot dismiss him, because Eliot won't let you.
She keeps insisting on his genuine love for Maggie — that it is real, even as it maims her.
There's a line that has always struck me — where she describes Tom's love for Maggie as having something of the quality of a peremptory, exclusive affection.
He loves her the way a proprietor loves his finest possession — with pride, and without permission.
As a performer, that is devastating material — because the love is absolutely real and absolutely insufficient.
What you're describing is precisely what makes the novel so hard to re-read — in the best possible sense.
Because Eliot keeps giving you the child version of their relationship first.
She establishes this paradise of mutual need — Maggie desperate to be seen, Tom the sun she orbits.
And then she shows you how that paradise becomes the instrument of Maggie's suffering.
The fishing scene in the early chapters — Maggie forgetting to keep watch over the lines because she's absorbed in a book.
And Tom's cold withdrawal — not anger, but that particular frost of disappointment.
Eliot is already writing the adult relationship in miniature.
The pattern is all there — Tom withholds, Maggie crumbles, Maggie tries harder, Tom remains unmoved.
I want to defend Tom, at least partially — because I think he is persistently misread by sympathetic readers of Maggie.
Tom operates according to a coherent moral code.
It is a code of duty, of family honour, of keeping one's word — and by that code, he is exemplary.
He pays his father's debts when he needn't have done.
He works with extraordinary self-discipline and sacrifice to restore the family's name and reclaim Dorlcote Mill.
Now, Eliot does not endorse his code — she is far too subtle for that.
But she shows us that his failures toward Maggie are inseparable from his virtues — and that is the real tragedy.
Edmund, I take the point — but doesn't it rather make it worse?
If Tom were simply cruel and selfish, Maggie could leave him behind emotionally.
But because his code is genuinely honourable in its way, she can never dismiss it — she can only fail it, over and over.
Think of the scene after the elopement with Stephen Guest — Tom's judgement of her.
He tells her she is no longer his sister.
And he means it — not as rhetoric, but as a verdict.
On the stage, that moment would require absolute stillness — no actor can play it with anger.
The horror is precisely in its calm.
That scene is almost unbearable to read.
Because what Eliot does — and this is her great cruelty as a novelist — is make us understand Tom completely in that moment.
She goes into his consciousness and shows you his genuine devastation — his sense of betrayal.
He has worked and sacrificed to restore the family name — and in his view, she has destroyed it.
And then Eliot turns the lens back to Maggie — and we feel the sentence land on her.
She describes Maggie's response as a great wave of anguish — but underneath it, the terrible need for his approval has not died.
Even there. Even then.
What Eliot is anatomising, I think, is the way that childhood love becomes a kind of tyranny — not through malice, but through fixity of character.
Tom cannot change because he has no inner life that would permit change.
This is Eliot's most exact and devastating observation about a certain kind of Englishman — not a bad man, but a bounded one.
She writes somewhere that Tom had the unintelligent bliss of a stronger will resting on a stronger nature — something very close to that.
The word 'unintelligent' does an enormous amount of work there — it is not stupidity, exactly.
It is the absence of self-examination — the incapacity to wonder whether one might be wrong.
And that is what makes the ending so completely right, dramatically speaking — and so shattering.
The flood comes — and it dissolves the fixity.
For the first time, Tom is stripped of everything — his mill, his position, his moral certainty — and all that is left is the child who loved Maggie.
His last word to her — 'Maggie' — spoken across the water.
It's the only word that needed to be said.
And Eliot ends them together — as they began.
In the boat, in the water, the past and the present fused — Tom's arm around her, and then the flood takes them both.
She earns that ending in a way few novelists could.
Because she has spent the whole novel insisting on the impossibility of the reconciliation — and then the flood makes it possible.
Not because Tom has changed — he hasn't, not really.
But because the catastrophe has stripped away everything that made change necessary.
The novel's epigraph promises that — 'in their death they were not divided.'
In their death they were not divided.
It's from the Book of Samuel — and Eliot chose it knowing exactly what she was doing.
It is the only resolution the novel could grant them — and it breaks your heart completely.
The flood as both catastrophe and grace — that's a tension Eliot holds with remarkable steadiness.
Edmund, I want to come back to something you said — about the virtues being inseparable from the failures.
Does that apply to Maggie as well — are her failures inseparable from her particular kind of goodness?
Entirely so — and that is where I think Eliot's moral imagination is at its finest.
Maggie's defining quality is the intensity of her need for love — an appetite for sympathy that she herself recognises as a weakness.
And it is the same quality that makes her capable of extraordinary generosity, extraordinary self-sacrifice.
Her renunciation of Stephen Guest — whatever one thinks of the precise decision — comes from that same deep well.
She gives up happiness because she cannot bear to have purchased it at Philip's expense, at Lucy's expense.
The same sensitivity that makes her suffer so acutely under Tom's judgement makes her incapable of causing that suffering to others.
And yet — the irony Eliot plants so carefully — she does cause suffering.
Not through malice, but through her very incapacity for half-measures.
Philip Wakem loves her, and she lets herself be loved in that half-lit way — visiting him secretly in the Red Deeps.
She doesn't intend injury — but the injury comes anyway.
Eliot is ruthless on this point — intentions do not protect us from our consequences.
The Red Deeps scenes are some of the most quietly beautiful writing in the whole novel.
There's something almost Pre-Raphaelite about them — that dappled, enclosed, out-of-time quality.
And Philip, of course, is the one person who truly sees Maggie — who reads her accurately and loves what he reads.
Which makes Tom's discovery of those meetings — and his contemptuous destruction of them — one of the cruelest scenes in Victorian fiction.
He forces Maggie to promise never to see Philip again.
Not because he has considered Philip's character, or Philip's worth — but because Philip is a Wakem.
Tom's moral seriousness and his small-mindedness are, as Edmund says, completely fused.
The Wakem enmity — inherited, irrational, and utterly destructive.
There's something almost Shakespearean in the way that family feud shadows the younger generation.
Oliver — final thought on the relationship between Tom and Maggie?
My final thought is this: every great sibling story in literature is about the impossibility of being seen accurately by the person who knew you first.
Tom knew Maggie before she became herself — and he never updated the record.
She remained, for him, the difficult, wayward, disobedient little sister — forever.
And Maggie's great tragedy is that she kept trying to revise that record — kept hoping the Tom she remembered from childhood would somehow reappear.
In the flood, he does.
For exactly long enough.
For exactly long enough.
In our next segment, we turn to the other great bond in Maggie's life — her relationship with Philip Wakem, and the question of whether intellectual sympathy can substitute for a more complete love.

segments.title: The Pen's Precision: How Eliot Builds a World

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this episode we'll be pulling apart one of the great novels of the Victorian age — and arguably of any age.
George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss is a novel of extraordinary precision — precise in its geography, its social comedy, its psychology, and its grief.
To help us unpack it, I'm joined by three guests who bring wonderfully different eyes to this book.

Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic novel recordings than almost anyone alive — he comes to fiction the way a musician comes to a score, listening for what the prose wants to do.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished literary minds of his generation — a reader who believes the novel's ultimate business is moral imagination, and who will not let us forget it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times since — she's our guide to what it actually feels like on the page.
We begin with the question of world-building — because before Eliot does anything else, she builds a world of almost suffocating completeness.
Oliver, you've read this novel aloud more times than most people have read it silently — where does that world begin for you?
It begins with a dreamer standing at a window, watching a river.
The novel opens in a kind of waking reverie — a narrator who tells us they are looking at the River Floss, the Dorlcote Mill, the water-wheel turning.
And then the child appears — a small figure with dark hair, standing at the edge of the water, doing absolutely nothing plot-wise.
What Eliot is doing there, right at the outset, is something I find endlessly instructive as a performer.
She is teaching you how to look.
The prose has this quality of patient, almost hypnotic attention — it won't be rushed into story.
And when you read it aloud, you feel the reader being slowed down, drawn in, almost physically lowered into that landscape.
That opening is, in its way, a piece of theatre before the play begins.
Oliver is quite right about the slowness — but I'd frame the achievement rather differently.
What Eliot is doing in those opening pages is establishing moral geography before she establishes plot geography.
St. Ogg's is not simply a backdrop — it is a community with a history, with unwritten laws, with a corporate memory of what is done and what is not done.
Eliot gives us the legend of St. Ogg himself in Book First — this ferryman who carried the Virgin across the river and was blessed for his charity.
That legend is not decoration.
It plants at the centre of the novel's world a question about mercy — about who in this town will extend it, and to whom, and at what cost.
The world Eliot builds is not merely atmospheric — it is ethically loaded from the very first pages.
What strikes me, reading it again and again, is how much of that world is carried by the prose texture itself.

There's a sentence I come back to constantly — in the early chapters, where Eliot describes the Tullivers' world as belonging to 'the lanes and the fields' rather than to what she calls the 'oppressive gentility' of the town.
And you feel that phrase — 'oppressive gentility' — doing real social work.
She doesn't say 'the middle classes are anxious and conformist' — she finds two words that make you feel the texture of that anxiety in your chest.
That is what I mean when I say Eliot builds a world — not just that she describes it accurately, but that she makes it physically present through language.
You don't observe St. Ogg's from outside — you find yourself inside it, breathing its particular air.
Caroline, yes — and I think the character who most embodies that world-building precision is Mrs. Tulliver.
Not Tom, not Maggie — Mrs. Tulliver, who is magnificently comic and magnificently limited in almost the same breath.
Her great concern in the early chapters is the linen — the sheets, the tablecloths, the items she brought as her 'chiny' into the marriage.
There's a passage where she enumerates these possessions with a grief that is entirely genuine — and Eliot plays it perfectly straight, which is what makes it so funny and so sad at once.
When you perform that kind of writing you have to trust the novelist completely — not wink at the audience, not signal that Mrs. Tulliver is foolish.
Because Eliot doesn't think she's foolish — she thinks Mrs. Tulliver's devotion to her household gods is as real and as worthy of attention as anything else in this novel.
That evenhandedness of attention is, for me, the signature of the great novelist.
Oliver touches on something that I think is often undervalued — Eliot's comedy.
The Dodson aunts — Mrs. Glegg, Mrs. Pullet, Mrs. Deane — are drawn with a satirical precision that would not embarrass Trollope.
Mrs. Glegg's sense of her own moral superiority — expressed always through the management of money and the strategic withholding of affection — is a complete social portrait in miniature.
But I'd push back gently on the idea that this is merely world-building as atmosphere.
The Dodsons exist in the novel to represent a complete moral system — a coherent, if narrow, code by which life is to be lived and judged.
Eliot is not simply decorating her novel with amusing types — she is staging a collision between competing notions of what it means to live rightly.
And St. Ogg's is the arena in which that collision plays out, over two generations.
Edmund's point about competing moral systems leads me to what I think is Eliot's most audacious move in the world-building.

There's a remarkable passage in Book Fourth — the chapter called 'A Variation of Protestantism Unknown to Bossuet' — where the narrator steps back and reflects on the culture of the Dodsons and Tullivers directly.

Eliot argues there that this provincial world has its own complete internal logic — its own religion, almost — centred on decent behaviour, family obligation, and the proper management of material things.
She is making a startlingly sympathetic case for a world she is also, in the same breath, satirising.
That double vision — holding satire and sympathy simultaneously — is, for me, the technical achievement at the heart of the novel's world.
It is very hard to do.
Most novelists choose one or the other — Eliot insists on both.
That double vision extends to the prose rhythm as well — which I think is underappreciated.
Eliot's sentences can shift register within a single clause — from something almost biblical in its gravity to something sharply, drily comic.
There's a sentence early on where she describes Mr. Tulliver as a man with a 'warm heart and a good-natured vanity' — and that pairing does everything.
'A warm heart and a good-natured vanity.'
You've got the man's whole character in six words — his generosity and his foolishness and the way one feeds the other.
That's the precision Caroline was talking about — not describing characters from outside but finding the phrase that contains them.
When you read that aloud you feel it click into place.
Mr. Tulliver is in fact one of Eliot's finest achievements — precisely because he is not merely comic.
His obstinacy, his lawsuits, his conviction that the world has dealt him unfairly — these are flaws that carry genuine tragic weight.

There is a scene — when Tulliver, having lost the mill and been broken by debt, recovers sufficiently to write in the family Bible — that is, for me, among the most quietly devastating passages in Victorian fiction.
He writes down his wish that Tom will remember the wrong done to him — this act of a broken man trying to extend his grievance beyond death.
And Eliot does not judge him for it.
She shows us the pathos of a man whose only instrument of power is a pencil entry in a family record.
That is world-building of the deepest kind — revealing the entire social architecture through one man's wounded pride.
I want to come back to Maggie in all of this — because I think the world-building ultimately exists for her sake.
Every social detail, every Dodson aunt, every inch of the Floss and the mill and the Red Deeps — it all exists to create the weight that Maggie is trying to carry, and sometimes trying to escape.
Eliot gives us that famous line about Maggie's need for love — that she was 'like a too-eager retriever' in her thirst for affection.
'Like a too-eager retriever.'
It's funny and it's heartbreaking — and it could only land the way it does because we already inhabit the world that has made Maggie so hungry.
The precision of the world-building is, finally, a form of compassion.
You cannot feel what Maggie's entrapment costs her unless you have lived in that world first.
Compassion as precision — that may be the finest summary of Eliot's method I've heard.
We've been thinking about how the world of St. Ogg's is assembled — its moral geography, its comic types, its prose texture, the weight it places on those who live inside it.

In the next part of our conversation, we'll turn to the figure at the centre of it all — Maggie Tulliver herself, and the question of what the novel imagines for a girl of her nature in a world of this kind.

segments.title: Love, Loss, and the Waters Rising

utterances.text: We have spent this episode inside the world that George Eliot built with such extraordinary care — the mill, the river, the family, the town.
And now we arrive at the place where all of that care culminates — the flood, and the ending that readers have argued about for over a hundred and fifty years.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — the waters are rising.
The flood has always seemed to me the most audacious thing George Eliot does in this novel — and she does a great many audacious things.
She has spent six books — six! — building a world of almost suffocating social realism.
And then she ends it with a catastrophe that arrives from outside all of that — from nature, from the river itself.
There is something almost mythic about it.
The Floss doesn't just kill Maggie — it answers something in her.
I think one must resist the temptation to make the flood purely symbolic, as if Eliot were writing a poem rather than a novel.
The flood is a catastrophe, yes — but what gives it its moral weight is what it forces Maggie to do.
She rows out into the darkness to rescue Tom.
Whatever the quarrel between them — and it has been fierce and prolonged — she goes to him first.
That is a moral act. That is character revealed under pressure — which is, in the end, the only thing a novelist can really show us.
What moves me most about that scene — every single time I read it — is the moment Tom sees Maggie coming toward him across the water.
Eliot writes that Tom's eyes fill with tears, and that he calls out her name — and the years of coldness and cruelty just dissolve.
She gives him back his sister in the last minutes of his life.
And Eliot gives us those four words — 'in their death they were not divided' — carved on their tombstone at the close.
in their death they were not divided
It's from the Book of Samuel, of course — Saul and Jonathan — and Eliot places it there deliberately, enormously.
And it earns that allusion, I think — which is the extraordinary thing.
Because the whole novel has been about the love between Maggie and Tom — this ferocious, unequal, inextinguishable thing.
Tom has been harsh, even monstrous at moments.
He casts Maggie out after the elopement with Stephen Guest — utterly, finally — and yet she cannot stop loving him.
Eliot makes us feel the pull of that bond as almost a physical thing — like the current of the Floss itself.
Tom is a character critics have been rather unkind to, and I confess I don't entirely agree with the prosecution.
He is rigid, yes. He is morally severe in a way that causes great suffering.
But he is also the one who sacrifices years of his life to redeem his father's debts — to restore the family honour.
Eliot is not asking us simply to condemn Tom — she is asking us to understand what makes a person like Tom possible.
What combination of upbringing, and culture, and narrow formation of mind produces that particular kind of painful goodness.
And Maggie understands it — that's the thing that breaks your heart.
She never stops seeing Tom clearly, and she never stops loving what is good in him, even as he wounds her repeatedly.
There is a passage early in the novel where Eliot describes Maggie's need for love as something almost desperate — she says Maggie would have given up half her future to be sure that Tom loved her.
'She would have given up half her future for the sake of being certain that Tom loved her.'
That sentence lives in me. It always has.
And the Stephen Guest episode — which so many readers find difficult — I think it's essential to that same hunger.
Maggie is not a fool. She knows Philip Wakem loves her truly, and she values that love.
But Stephen Guest is — whatever one thinks of him — overwhelmingly present, physically, socially, emotionally.
And Eliot has the nerve to show us a Maggie who is genuinely swept away — not because she is weak, but because she is human.
The novel doesn't flinch from the bodily reality of attraction — which in 1860 was a rather remarkable thing to put on the page.
The Stephen Guest controversy is one of the few critical arguments about this novel that I find genuinely wearisome.
Whether Stephen is an adequate object for Maggie's passion is, to my mind, precisely the point.
Great passion is rarely directed at perfectly adequate objects — that is rather the nature of passion.
What matters is Maggie's choice — her decision to return, to refuse the drift downriver, to come back and face the consequences.
That return is the moral centre of the novel, not the flood.
I agree with Edmund about the return — and yet the flood still feels necessary to me, not as escape but as completion.
Maggie has always been in tension with St Ogg's — too large for it, too hungry, too alive.
And the river has always been there — present from the very first page, shaping everything.
Eliot opens the novel with the narrator dreaming beside the Floss in winter — watching the water, watching the mill.
The ending doesn't contradict that opening — it fulfils it.
And that opening is one of the most beautiful in all Victorian fiction, isn't it.
Eliot establishes from the first sentence that this story belongs to memory — to the half-dreaming recovery of a world that is gone.
She writes: 'A wide plain, where the broadening Floss hurries on between its green banks to the sea.'
'A wide plain, where the broadening Floss hurries on between its green banks to the sea.'
And we are already in it. We are already lost in it.
A novel that begins in water and ends in water — and in between, a whole human life, fierce and tender and irreducible.
Oliver, Edmund, Caroline — I want to end simply by asking each of you: what do you carry away from The Mill on the Floss?
What I carry away is something that has always seemed to me underappreciated — Eliot's profound sympathy for those who fail.
Not the heroic failures — not Maggie alone — but Mr Tulliver, ruined by a lawsuit and by his own fierce pride.
Mrs Tulliver, clinging to her china and her linen as the world contracts around her.
Eliot never condescends to these people. She sees them whole.
I carry away Maggie — always Maggie.
The Maggie of the attic with her wooden doll, hammering nails into it when the world became too much.
The Maggie of the Red Deeps, talking with Philip, hungry for books and ideas that no one around her thought she needed.
The Maggie who rows out into the flood in the dark.
She is one of the great creations — not just of Victorian fiction, but of the novel entire.
I carry away the comedy, actually — and I won't apologise for it.
The Dodson aunts — Mrs Glegg, Mrs Pullet, Mrs Deane — with their hierarchies of linen and their views on proper grieving.
Mr Riley dispensing professional advice with magnificent confidence in his own ignorance.
Eliot sees the comedy and the pathos as the same thing — and that double vision is a kind of genius.
You laugh, and then you ache — sometimes at the very same sentence.
You laugh, and then you ache — I can't think of a finer summary of what it is to read George Eliot.
The Mill on the Floss — a novel about childhood, and ambition, and the weight of being loved imperfectly, and the river that runs through all of it.
Thank you to Oliver Trevelyan, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation full of care and pleasure.
And thank you, most of all, for listening.

c52:p2.text:
Maggie, all this time, moved about with a quiescence and even torpor of manner,
so contrasted with her usual fitful brightness and ardor, that Lucy would have
had to seek some other cause for such a change, if she had not been convinced
that the position in which Maggie stood between Philip and her brother, and the
prospect of her self-imposed wearisome banishment, were quite enough to account
for a large amount of depression. But under this torpor there was a fierce
battle of emotions, such as Maggie in all her life of struggle had never known
or foreboded; it seemed to her as if all the worst evil in her had lain in
ambush till now, and had suddenly started up full-armed, with hideous,
overpowering strength! There were moments in which a cruel selfishness seemed
to be getting possession of her; why should not Lucy, why should not Philip,
suffer?  She  had had to suffer through many years of her life; and who
had renounced anything for her? And when something like that fulness of
existence—love, wealth, ease, refinement, all that her nature
craved—was brought within her reach, why was she to forego it, that
another might have it,—another, who perhaps needed it less? But amidst
all this new passionate tumult there were the old voices making themselves
heard with rising power, till, from time to time, the tumult seemed quelled.
 Was  that existence which tempted her the full existence she dreamed?
Where, then, would be all the memories of early striving; all the deep pity for
another’s pain, which had been nurtured in her through years of affection
and hardship; all the divine presentiment of something higher than mere
personal enjoyment, which had made the sacredness of life? She might as well
hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in
which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs
of her soul. And then, if pain were so hard to  her , what was it to
others? “Ah, God! preserve me from inflicting—give me strength to
bear it.” How had she sunk into this struggle with a temptation that she
would once have thought herself as secure from as from deliberate crime? When
was that first hateful moment in which she had been conscious of a feeling that
clashed with her truth, affection, and gratitude, and had not shaken it from
her with horror, as if it had been a loathsome thing? And yet, since this
strange, sweet, subduing influence did not, should not, conquer
her,—since it was to remain simply her own suffering,—her mind was
meeting Stephen’s in that thought of his, that they might still snatch
moments of mute confession before the parting came. For was not he suffering
too? She saw it daily—saw it in the sickened look of fatigue with which,
as soon as he was not compelled to exert himself, he relapsed into indifference
toward everything but the possibility of watching her. Could she refuse
sometimes to answer that beseeching look which she felt to be following her
like a low murmur of love and pain? She refused it less and less, till at last
the evening for them both was sometimes made of a moment’s mutual gaze;
they thought of it till it came, and when it had come, they thought of nothing
else.
c52:p2.summary: Maggie experiences an unprecedented internal battle between cruel selfish impulses and her moral conscience, as the narrator reveals her struggle between personal happiness and loyalty to Lucy and Philip through a passage of intense philosophical introspection.

He very soon set down poor Tom as a thoroughly stupid lad; for though by hard
labour he could get particular declensions into his brain, anything so abstract
as the relation between cases and terminations could by no means get such a
lodgment there as to enable him to recognise a chance genitive or dative. This
struck Mr Stelling as something more than natural stupidity; he suspected
obstinacy, or at any rate indifference, and lectured Tom severely on his want
of thorough application. “You feel no interest in what you’re
doing, sir,” Mr Stelling would say, and the reproach was painfully true.
Tom had never found any difficulty in discerning a pointer from a setter, when
once he had been told the distinction, and his perceptive powers were not at
all deficient. I fancy they were quite as strong as those of the Rev. Mr
Stelling; for Tom could predict with accuracy what number of horses were
cantering behind him, he could throw a stone right into the centre of a given
ripple, he could guess to a fraction how many lengths of his stick it would
take to reach across the playground, and could draw almost perfect squares on
his slate without any measurement. But Mr Stelling took no note of these
things; he only observed that Tom’s faculties failed him before the
abstractions hideously symbolised to him in the pages of the Eton Grammar, and
that he was in a state bordering on idiocy with regard to the demonstration
that two given triangles must be equal, though he could discern with great
promptitude and certainty the fact that they  were  equal. Whence Mr
Stelling concluded that Tom’s brain, being peculiarly impervious to
etymology and demonstrations, was peculiarly in need of being ploughed and
harrowed by these patent implements; it was his favourite metaphor, that the
classics and geometry constituted that culture of the mind which prepared it
for the reception of any subsequent crop. I say nothing against Mr
Stelling’s theory; if we are to have one regimen for all minds, his seems
to me as good as any other. I only know it turned out as uncomfortably for Tom
Tulliver as if he had been plied with cheese in order to remedy a gastric
weakness which prevented him from digesting it. It is astonishing what a
different result one gets by changing the metaphor! Once call the brain an
intellectual stomach, and one’s ingenious conception of the classics and
geometry as ploughs and harrows seems to settle nothing. But then it is open to
some one else to follow great authorities, and call the mind a sheet of white
paper or a mirror, in which case one’s knowledge of the digestive process
becomes quite irrelevant. It was doubtless an ingenious idea to call the camel
the ship of the desert, but it would hardly lead one far in training that
useful beast. O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being “the
freshest modern” instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have
mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence,
with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without
metaphor,—that we can so seldom declare what a thing is, except by saying
it is something else?

Yet, strange to say, under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl
than he had ever been in his life before. He had a large share of pride, which
had hitherto found itself very comfortable in the world, despising Old Goggles,
and reposing in the sense of unquestioned rights; but now this same pride met
with nothing but bruises and crushings. Tom was too clear-sighted not to be
aware that Mr Stelling’s standard of things was quite different, was
certainly something higher in the eyes of the world than that of the people he
had been living amongst, and that, brought in contact with it, he, Tom
Tulliver, appeared uncouth and stupid; he was by no means indifferent to this,
and his pride got into an uneasy condition which quite nullified his boyish
self-satisfaction, and gave him something of the girl’s susceptibility.
He was of a very firm, not to say obstinate, disposition, but there was no
brute-like rebellion and recklessness in his nature; the human sensibilities
predominated, and if it had occurred to him that he could enable himself to
show some quickness at his lessons, and so acquire Mr Stelling’s
approbation, by standing on one leg for an inconvenient length of time, or
rapping his head moderately against the wall, or any voluntary action of that
sort, he would certainly have tried it. But no; Tom had never heard that these
measures would brighten the understanding, or strengthen the verbal memory; and
he was not given to hypothesis and experiment. It did occur to him that he
could perhaps get some help by praying for it; but as the prayers he said every
evening were forms learned by heart, he rather shrank from the novelty and
irregularity of introducing an extempore passage on a topic of petition for
which he was not aware of any precedent. But one day, when he had broken down,
for the fifth time, in the supines of the third conjugation, and Mr Stelling,
convinced that this must be carelessness, since it transcended the bounds of
possible stupidity, had lectured him very seriously, pointing out that if he
failed to seize the present golden opportunity of learning supines, he would
have to regret it when he became a man,—Tom, more miserable than usual,
determined to try his sole resource; and that evening, after his usual form of
prayer for his parents and “little sister” (he had begun to pray
for Maggie when she was a baby), and that he might be able always to keep
God’s commandments, he added, in the same low whisper, “and please
to make me always remember my Latin.” He paused a little to consider how
he should pray about Euclid—whether he should ask to see what it meant,
or whether there was any other mental state which would be more applicable to
the case. But at last he added: “And make Mr Stelling say I
sha’n’t do Euclid any more. Amen.”

This time of utmost need was come to Maggie, with her short span of thirteen
years. To the usual precocity of the girl, she added that early experience of
struggle, of conflict between the inward impulse and outward fact, which is the
lot of every imaginative and passionate nature; and the years since she
hammered the nails into her wooden Fetish among the worm-eaten shelves of the
attic had been filled with so eager a life in the triple world of Reality,
Books, and Waking Dreams, that Maggie was strangely old for her years in
everything except in her entire want of that prudence and self-command which
were the qualities that made Tom manly in the midst of his intellectual
boyishness. And now her lot was beginning to have a still, sad monotony, which
threw her more than ever on her inward self. Her father was able to attend to
business again, his affairs were settled, and he was acting as Wakem’s
manager on the old spot. Tom went to and fro every morning and evening, and
became more and more silent in the short intervals at home; what was there to
say? One day was like another; and Tom’s interest in life, driven back
and crushed on every other side, was concentrating itself into the one channel
of ambitious resistance to misfortune. The peculiarities of his father and
mother were very irksome to him, now they were laid bare of all the softening
accompaniments of an easy, prosperous home; for Tom had very clear, prosaic
eyes, not apt to be dimmed by mists of feeling or imagination. Poor Mrs
Tulliver, it seemed, would never recover her old self, her placid household
activity; how could she? The objects among which her mind had moved
complacently were all gone,—all the little hopes and schemes and
speculations, all the pleasant little cares about her treasures which had made
the world quite comprehensible to her for a quarter of a century, since she had
made her first purchase of the sugar-tongs, had been suddenly snatched away
from her, and she remained bewildered in this empty life. Why that should have
happened to her which had not happened to other women remained an insoluble
question by which she expressed her perpetual ruminating comparison of the past
with the present. It was piteous to see the comely woman getting thinner and
more worn under a bodily as well as mental restlessness, which made her often
wander about the empty house after her work was done, until Maggie, becoming
alarmed about her, would seek her, and bring her down by telling her how it
vexed Tom that she was injuring her health by never sitting down and resting
herself. Yet amidst this helpless imbecility there was a touching trait of
humble, self-devoting maternity, which made Maggie feel tenderly toward her
poor mother amidst all the little wearing griefs caused by her mental
feebleness. She would let Maggie do none of the work that was heaviest and most
soiling to the hands, and was quite peevish when Maggie attempted to relieve
her from her grate-brushing and scouring: “Let it alone, my dear; your
hands ’ull get as hard as hard,” she would say; “it’s
your mother’s place to do that. I can’t do the sewing—my eyes
fail me.” And she would still brush and carefully tend Maggie’s
hair, which she had become reconciled to, in spite of its refusal to curl, now
it was so long and massy. Maggie was not her pet child, and, in general, would
have been much better if she had been quite different; yet the womanly heart,
so bruised in its small personal desires, found a future to rest on in the life
of this young thing, and the mother pleased herself with wearing out her own
hands to save the hands that had so much more life in them.
c31:p1.summary: Maggie, precocious and imaginative, now faces a dreary family life after financial ruin; Tom retreats into silent ambition to repay debts, while Mrs Tulliver declines into bewildered apathy, yet shows tender maternal care for her daughter.

c31:p3.text:
Mr Tulliver lingered nowhere away from home; he hurried away from market, he
refused all invitations to stay and chat, as in old times, in the houses where
he called on business. He could not be reconciled with his lot. There was no
attitude in which his pride did not feel its bruises; and in all behaviour
toward him, whether kind or cold, he detected an allusion to the change in his
circumstances. Even the days on which Wakem came to ride round the land and
inquire into the business were not so black to him as those market-days on
which he had met several creditors who had accepted a composition from him. To
save something toward the repayment of those creditors was the object toward
which he was now bending all his thoughts and efforts; and under the influence
of this all-compelling demand of his nature, the somewhat profuse man, who
hated to be stinted or to stint any one else in his own house, was gradually
metamorphosed into the keen-eyed grudger of morsels. Mrs Tulliver could not
economise enough to satisfy him, in their food and firing; and he would eat
nothing himself but what was of the coarsest quality. Tom, though depressed and
strongly repelled by his father’s sullenness, and the dreariness of home,
entered thoroughly into his father’s feelings about paying the creditors;
and the poor lad brought his first quarter’s money, with a delicious
sense of achievement, and gave it to his father to put into the tin box which
held the savings. The little store of sovereigns in the tin box seemed to be
the only sight that brought a faint beam of pleasure into the miller’s
eyes,—faint and transient, for it was soon dispelled by the thought that
the time would be long—perhaps longer than his life,—before the
narrow savings could remove the hateful incubus of debt. A deficit of more than
five hundred pounds, with the accumulating interest, seemed a deep pit to fill
with the savings from thirty shillings a-week, even when Tom’s probable
savings were to be added. On this one point there was entire community of
feeling in the four widely differing beings who sat round the dying fire of
sticks, which made a cheap warmth for them on the verge of bedtime. Mrs
Tulliver carried the proud integrity of the Dodsons in her blood, and had been
brought up to think that to wrong people of their money, which was another
phrase for debt, was a sort of moral pillory; it would have been wickedness, to
her mind, to have run counter to her husband’s desire to “do the
right thing,” and retrieve his name. She had a confused, dreamy notion
that, if the creditors were all paid, her plate and linen ought to come back to
her; but she had an inbred perception that while people owed money they were
unable to pay, they couldn’t rightly call anything their own. She
murmured a little that Mr Tulliver so peremptorily refused to receive anything
in repayment from Mr and Mrs Moss; but to all his requirements of household
economy she was submissive to the point of denying herself the cheapest
indulgences of mere flavour; her only rebellion was to smuggle into the kitchen
something that would make rather a better supper than usual for Tom.
c31:p3.summary: Mr Tulliver's pride is wounded by his changed circumstances; driven by moral duty to repay creditors, he becomes austere and grudging, finding grim solace in accumulated savings while the family suffers privation.
c31:p3.best_quote: the somewhat profuse man, who hated to be stinted or to stint any one else in his own house, was gradually metamorphosed into the keen-eyed grudger of morsels

c33:p2.text:
It was far on in June now, and Maggie was inclined to lengthen the daily walk
which was her one indulgence; but this day and the following she was so busy
with work which must be finished that she never went beyond the gate, and
satisfied her need of the open air by sitting out of doors. One of her frequent
walks, when she was not obliged to go to St Ogg’s, was to a spot that
lay beyond what was called the “Hill,”—an insignificant rise
of ground crowned by trees, lying along the side of the road which ran by the
gates of Dorlcote Mill. Insignificant I call it, because in height it was
hardly more than a bank; but there may come moments when Nature makes a mere
bank a means toward a fateful result; and that is why I ask you to imagine this
high bank crowned with trees, making an uneven wall for some quarter of a mile
along the left side of Dorlcote Mill and the pleasant fields behind it, bounded
by the murmuring Ripple. Just where this line of bank sloped down again to the
level, a by-road turned off and led to the other side of the rise, where it was
broken into very capricious hollows and mounds by the working of an exhausted
stone-quarry, so long exhausted that both mounds and hollows were now clothed
with brambles and trees, and here and there by a stretch of grass which a few
sheep kept close-nibbled. In her childish days Maggie held this place, called
the Red Deeps, in very great awe, and needed all her confidence in Tom’s
bravery to reconcile her to an excursion thither,—visions of robbers and
fierce animals haunting every hollow. But now it had the charm for her which
any broken ground, any mimic rock and ravine, have for the eyes that rest
habitually on the level; especially in summer, when she could sit on a grassy
hollow under the shadow of a branching ash, stooping aslant from the steep
above her, and listen to the hum of insects, like tiniest bells on the garment
of Silence, or see the sunlight piercing the distant boughs, as if to chase and
drive home the truant heavenly blue of the wild hyacinths. In this June time,
too, the dog-roses were in their glory, and that was an additional reason why
Maggie should direct her walk to the Red Deeps, rather than to any other spot,
on the first day she was free to wander at her will,—a pleasure she loved
so well, that sometimes, in her ardors of renunciation, she thought she ought
to deny herself the frequent indulgence in it.
c33:p2.summary: Maggie's favourite haunt, the Red Deeps, is described with rich sensory detail; the narrator hints that this location holds fateful significance.
c33:p2.best_quote: Nature makes a mere bank a means toward a fateful result
